start.lead: People left machines on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Nine of the ten went quiet long ago. One still does its job. This is a tour of all ten, with the real data for this exact second.
start.sendBody: Hold the button. A real signal travels at the speed of light, and we will tell you when it reaches each machine, all the way out to Pioneer 10.
start.again: Hold to send a new signal

echo.title: One of them answers.
echo.body: On the Moon there is a small mirror from Apollo 14. It needs no power, so it never stopped working. Telescopes on Earth still fire lasers at it and time the echo. Try it yourself: the wait is real, not sped up.
dust.title: Then the sky went dark.
dust.body: A dust storm covered the whole planet. Opportunity ran on sunlight. Scientists measure how dusty the sky is with a number called tau.
dust.storm: 10 June 2018, the last value Opportunity measured
dust.end: That day, Opportunity called home for the last time. Its team tried to wake it for eight months.
dust.myth: People say its last words were
dust.quote: “My battery is low and it's getting dark.”
dust.truth: Rovers don't send sentences. They send numbers. A science reporter turned those numbers into words. It is still a beautiful line.

finale.lead: Ten machines. One question: who is still out there? Each answers in its own voice, in the order it went quiet.

about.scale.body: In the 3D view, the worlds and machines are not to scale, so that you can see them all. Every machine stands at its real latitude and longitude, and each world is lit by the Sun exactly as it is right now. The clock during each flight shows the real light-travel time.
start.line: Ten machines are still out there. Nine stopped talking long ago. Let's call them.

world.deep.line: Bonus stop: two machines that never landed anywhere. Both are still moving away.

scroll.learned.surveyor3: It dug four trenches to test the Moon's soil and sent home 6,326 pictures. Two years later, Apollo 12 landed about 180 m away.
scroll.learned.eagle: It carried the first people to walk on the Moon. They brought home 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil.
scroll.learned.lrv: Astronauts could drive far for the first time: 27.8 km on Apollo 15, bringing back 77.31 kg of rock and soil.
scroll.learned.retro: Lasers bounced off it show the Moon moves 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year, and that the Moon has a fluid core.
scroll.learned.sojourner: It was the first rover on another planet. Rounded pebbles at its landing site suggest water once flowed there, in a warmer past.
scroll.learned.opportunity: It found hematite and tiny 'blueberries' that form in water: proof that water once stood on the surface of Mars.
scroll.learned.insight: It heard 1,319 marsquakes and used them to look inside Mars, at its crust, mantle and core.
scroll.learned.ingenuity: It made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet, then flew 72 times. Designed for 5 flights, it flew 17 km in all.
scroll.learned.kepler: It found more than 2,600 planets around other stars, and showed our galaxy has more planets than stars.
scroll.learned.pioneer10: It was the first to fly through the asteroid belt and past Jupiter, and the first human-made object to go beyond Neptune.
scroll.now.title: Where it is today
scroll.now.far: There is no picture of where it is today: it is far too far away for any camera to see.
scroll.now.eagle: Tranquility Base seen from orbit by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter in 2009. The arrows point to Eagle's descent stage and the experiments Apollo 11 left behind.
scroll.now.surveyor3: The Apollo 12 site seen from orbit by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Surveyor 3 still sits in its crater; Apollo 12's descent stage, Intrepid, is nearby.
scroll.now.lrv: Apollo 15's rover is still parked where the astronauts left it, seen from orbit by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter from just 25 km up. Look for its tracks.
scroll.now.retro: The Apollo 14 site from orbit. The arrow marks the science station the astronauts set up, near where the laser mirror stands; the dark lines are their footpaths, and the descent stage is on the right.
scroll.now.sojourner: Sojourner is too small to see clearly from orbit. This 1997 panorama marks where it was last seen. In 2006, an orbiter spotted a speck there about the size of the rover. It might be Sojourner, or just rocks: even NASA isn't sure.
scroll.now.opportunity: Opportunity is the blip in the square, seen by the HiRISE camera in orbit on 20 September 2018, after the dust storm had cleared. It never woke up.
scroll.now.insight: InSight seen from orbit by the HiRISE camera on 23 September 2019. You can make out its two round solar panels.
scroll.now.ingenuity: Ingenuity at its final airfield, nicknamed 'Valinor Hills', photographed by the Perseverance rover on 4 February 2024 from about 450 m away.
scroll.boot.hook: Right now, light from Earth takes {moon} to reach the Moon and {mars} to reach Mars. That's where we're going.
scroll.spot.how: This is a real photo from orbit. Tap where you think it is.

scroll.spot.eagle: The bright speck with a dark shadow is Eagle's bottom half, still where it landed in 1969.
scroll.spot.lrv: The dark spot at the end of the long line is the rover, parked where the astronauts left it. The line is the trail they left behind.
scroll.spot.retro: The tiny bright dot is the science station; the laser mirror is part of it. The dark path is the trail the astronauts walked.
scroll.spot.insight: The tiny blue-green speck is InSight. The dark patch around it is where its landing rockets blew the dust away.
